newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Journalists may testify in Singapore libel case.
newsitem.headline: Journalists may testify in Singapore libel case.

text.p: More than 50 people, mainly journalists, could be called to give evidence at a hearing to set costs against an opposition politician for defaming Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other ruling party members.
A lawyer for the plaintiffs said most of the people who might be called were local journalists and transcribers, but added some foreign journalists might also be asked to give evidence.
"We have a comprehensive list and now we are deciding on who to call," the lawyer told Reuters.
The libel suit is based on articles written by these journalists, said the lawyer, who declined to be identified.
He said the lawyers might not have to call anyone if the defendant, Tang Liang Hong, chose not to contest the hearings.
The case will be heard in the High Court on May 5.
Tang was found to have libelled Goh and other members of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), including former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, during Singapore's general election campaign in January.
The High Court had earlier ordered Tang and his wife to declare all their assets and to set aside Singapore $11.2 milion (US$7.9 million) to cover damages if he was found guilty.
Tang stood unsuccessfully for the opposition Worker's Party in the elections in which the PAP won 81 of 83 seats in parliament.
He fled Singapore shortly after the polls, saying he feared for his life.

During the campaign, the PAP accused Tang of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who threatened racial harmony in Singapore, where more than 70 percent of the population are ethnic Chinese but where there are also significant numbers of Malays and Indians.
Tang denied the allegations and said the PAP leaders had lied. He was hit by a deluge of 12 libel suits for these and other remarks, which were widely reported in local newspapers.
None of the newspapers has been sued for printing Tang's remarks.
